slides.headline: Finger catching or clicking?
slides.sub: What trigger finger is and what tends to help in the early stages.

slides.title: What's going on
slides.body: Trigger finger happens when a finger tendon doesn't glide smoothly through its tunnel at the base of the finger. It can catch, click or stick as you bend and straighten, often worse in the morning.

slides.title: Ease off the heavy gripping
slides.body: Repeated hard gripping, like tools, heavy bags or long gardening sessions, can aggravate it. Padding handles, swapping hands and breaking up tasks can give the tendon less to deal with.

slides.title: Keep it moving gently
slides.body: Gentle tendon gliding exercises, slowly moving the fingers through a few positions, can help keep things moving. Warm water in the morning often makes those first movements easier.

slides.title: Splinting can help some people
slides.body: A small splint that rests the affected finger, often worn overnight, can reduce catching for some people. A physio can advise on fit and how long to wear it each day.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: See your GP or physio if a finger locks and won't straighten, or becomes hot, red and swollen, especially after a cut. These need prompt attention rather than home care.

slides.headline: Get your grip back on track
slides.body: Our Sydney CBD and Chatswood physios assess your hand, look at your daily tasks and set up a plan, including splinting if it suits. Book online — link in bio.

caption:
Finger catching or clicking when you make a fist? It might be what's often called trigger finger.

It happens when a finger tendon doesn't glide smoothly through its tunnel at the base of the finger, so it catches as you bend and straighten. Mornings are often the stiffest.

Early on, a few simple things tend to help: easing off heavy or repeated gripping, padding tool handles, breaking up long tasks, gentle finger movements in warm water, and for some people a small splint worn overnight. A finger that locks and won't straighten, or one that turns hot, red and swollen, needs prompt attention.
